rationale: Re-derived the propose-time guard against the decoded history and the derivation contradicts the asserted trigger, so I narrow the claim to unresolved rather than leave it asserted. For a leader, becomeLeader sets pendingConfIndex to the last index at election, a proposal raises it to cover the change it appends, and the guard's alreadyPending clause blocks any later configuration change while applied is below it; if the leader has instead applied the committed joint change, its tracker is joint and the alreadyJoint clause blocks it. Every path I can construct to the decoded log - the first joint change appended by one leader, a second appended by the same leader after applying, by a new leader elected later, or by a node that restarted and then took office - is therefore blocked by one clause or the other, which means the receipt's history should not have been produced through stepLeader's MsgProp path with DisableConfChangeValidation at its default. I cannot yet say which of the two explanations holds: either there is a path I have not identified (for example an entry that reached the log some other way, or a node state the guard evaluates differently from my reading), or the sweep's history is an artefact of the harness's own bookkeeping. Until the proposer's state is observed at the moment the second change is appended, the availability claim cannot stand as asserted, and I record that narrowing with the observable that would settle it.

interpretations.rationale: What the receipts support is unchanged and remains on record: a joint-enter change that alters no membership still creates a joint configuration (index 17), the leave-joint entry needed to exit it is proposed only by a node that is leader when it applies the change (source, raft.go:742), the decoded history contains two joint-enter changes and no leave (indices 19-21), three nodes applied that history in order with reapplied_entry false and batch bounds at applied_before+1 or their first entry, and the second change is rejected with 'config is already joint', which applyConfChange turns into a process-fatal panic. What no longer holds is my assertion that this history is reachable through the target's own proposal path. Re-deriving the guard: a leader's pendingConfIndex is the last index at its election plus whatever changes it appends, so while its applied index is below that value alreadyPending blocks any new configuration change; and if its applied index has reached the committed joint change, its tracker is joint and alreadyJoint blocks it. I cannot construct a leader state that appends the second joint change - a later-elected leader inherits a pendingConfIndex covering the first change, and a restarted node that later takes office is reset to the same rule - so the decoded history should not have entered the log through stepLeader with DisableConfChangeValidation false. That leaves two possibilities and no observation to choose between them: a path I have not identified (an entry reaching the log by another route, or a guard evaluation differing from my reading of the code), or an artefact of the sweep's bookkeeping. The defect claim therefore returns to unresolved while the consequence chain stays documented, and the discriminator is concrete: instrument the sweep to record, at the moment a configuration change is appended, the appending node's pendingConfIndex, applied index, tracker jointness and whether DisableConfChangeValidation is set, and record the entry type and term of every log position in the rejected history (index 3 in particular, which the decoding leaves unexplained and which a later election's empty entry would explain).
counterevidence: The derivation is a source argument, not an observation, and the receipts contain states (index 17's no-op joint entry, index 16's stale-guard admission) that show the guard admits changes in states I constructed by hand; the sweep's history could involve a state of that kind that I have not enumerated.

The harness rebuilds nodes from persisted state at restart events and registers a node outside the configuration, so a bookkeeping path that produces a log the guard would not admit is plausible and is not excluded by the receipts.
violations=0 in every relevant receipt means the four checked invariants were unaffected either way, so the narrowing does not remove an observed safety result.
limitations: The concerning gap is the proposer-side state, which none of the receipts records; until it is recorded, neither the asserted nor the refuted reading is supported by execution.
The decoded history is capped at eight entries and the log position at index 3 has no explanation from the operands collected so far.

The consequence chain itself remains as documented: in-order application reaching an invalid change panics, which is the availability hazard the investigation set out to test, but a panic only matters if the history is reachable through permitted operations.
